after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 5 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-5\cdot (-5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-3)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 5 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & 5 \\ -5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-5\cdot (-5) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-3)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

after.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-1)(2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
content.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-1)(2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =-6,$ and

$$
J=A=-6I=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

Notice that $A$ is a scalar matrix, which means that it is already in Jordan canonical form. Therefore, it has a single (repeated) eigenvalue $\lambda =-5,$ and

$$
J=A=-5I=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

after.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -1 \\ 4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot (4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

content.problem:
Find the Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -1 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -1 \\ 4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-(-1)\cdot (4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ 

Since $A$ is not a scalar matrix, we conclude that $A$ is not diagonalizable, and its Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{2}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$
